clinicalPearls: Most common form of severe combined immunodeficiency, caused by mutations in IL2RG encoding the common gamma chain shared by the receptors for interleukins 2, 4, 7, 9, 15 and 21.

Immunophenotype is characteristically T-B+NK-: profoundly absent or non-functional T cells and natural killer cells, with B cells present in normal or raised numbers but incapable of effective antibody production.
X-linked recessive inheritance means affected infants are almost exclusively male; a family history of early male infant deaths from infection is a strong clue.
Presents in the first months of life with failure to thrive, persistent oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhoea, and recurrent or opportunistic infections including Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
Thymic shadow is typically absent on chest imaging and lymphoid tissue such as tonsils and lymph nodes is scanty or absent on examination.
Live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus, oral polio, MMR, varicella) and non-irradiated blood products are dangerous and can cause disseminated infection or transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative and outcomes are best when performed early before infections accumulate; gene therapy is an established alternative.
Newborn screening using T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) detects the near-absence of naive T cells and enables pre-symptomatic diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked SCID arises from loss-of-function mutations in IL2RG on the X chromosome, which encodes the common gamma chain (gamma-c). This chain is an indispensable signalling component shared across the receptors for interleukins 2, 4, 7, 9, 15 and 21, coupling ligand binding to the JAK3-STAT5 intracellular pathway. Absent interleukin-7 signalling halts thymic T-cell development, producing a profound deficiency of T lymphocytes, while absent interleukin-15 signalling abolishes natural killer cell development, giving the characteristic T-B+NK- pattern. B cells are generated normally in number but, deprived of T-cell help and defective in their own gamma-c-dependent interleukin-4 and interleukin-21 signalling, cannot undergo effective class switching or produce protective antibody. The net result is failure of both cellular and humoral adaptive immunity, rendering the infant susceptible to viral, fungal, bacterial and opportunistic organisms from the time maternal antibody wanes.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive JAK3 deficiency (phenocopy with identical T-B+NK- immunophenotype)
Interleukin-7 receptor alpha chain deficiency (T-B+NK+ SCID)
RAG1/RAG2 deficiency and Artemis deficiency (T-B-NK+ SCID)
Maternofoetal or acquired lymphopenia from congenital infection
Reticular dysgenesis with combined lymphoid and myeloid failure
additionalInvestigations: Lymphocyte subset enumeration by flow cytometry demonstrating the T-B+NK- pattern
Serum immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses (interpreted against transplacental maternal IgG)
T-cell proliferation assays to mitogens and antigens showing absent responses
IL2RG gene sequencing to confirm the causative mutation
Assessment of maternal engraftment and analysis of maternal X-inactivation as a carrier clue
TREC quantification confirming markedly reduced naive T-cell output
HLA typing of patient and family to expedite donor identification for transplantation
redFlags: Opportunistic infection such as Pneumocystis pneumonia or disseminated BCG in an infant
Persistent oral thrush and chronic diarrhoea with failure to thrive
Absent thymic shadow and impalpable lymphoid tissue
Erythroderma or hepatosplenomegaly suggesting maternal T-cell engraftment or transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease
Any male infant with severe lymphopenia and a family history of early male deaths
reference.prognosis: Untreated the condition is almost uniformly fatal within the first year or two of life from overwhelming infection. Early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy, particularly before significant infection burden accrues, offers excellent long-term survival and immune reconstitution.
pitfalls: Normal or raised total lymphocyte and B-cell counts can falsely reassure; naive T cells must be specifically assessed.
Transplacental maternal IgG can mask the humoral defect in early infancy, so normal immunoglobulins do not exclude the diagnosis.
Administering live vaccines or non-irradiated cellular blood products before diagnosis can be lethal.
Maternal T-cell engraftment may produce detectable circulating T cells and mislead interpretation of subsets.
Delaying transplantation to clear an active infection worsens outcomes; referral to a specialist centre should be immediate.
references: International primary immunodeficiency classification and management guidelines
National newborn screening and SCID management guidance
management: Urgent allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the definitive potentially curative treatment, ideally before significant infection accrues
Gene therapy directed at IL2RG as an alternative curative approach in suitable patients
Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole together with antifungal cover
Immunoglobulin replacement until immune reconstitution is achieved
Strict avoidance of live vaccines and use of irradiated, CMV-safe, leucodepleted blood products only
Protective isolation with aggressive treatment of intercurrent infection pending transplant
Newborn TREC-based screening and early referral to a specialist immunology transplant centre
Genetic counselling with IL2RG carrier testing of the mother and female relatives
